source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF p.2 explicitly links https://github.com/rajatvd/flash-sketch-arxiv. The local source inventory row still says no_public_source_found and corpus/visual_sources/icml-2026-c61e72161d50/ is absent, so the automatic candidate was independently checked with gh. gh repo view identifies the repository as code for the exact FlashSketch paper and its main tree contains the camera-ready, ablation, table and sketch-matrix generators listed above, plus paper/figures/appendix rendered assets. The source files give exact method HEX values, marker order, line widths, log-axis/ellipse logic and LaTeX table rules. No weights, datasets, checkpoints or full clone were fetched.

paper_style.palette_strategy: A source-exact categorical method palette is reused across all plots: FlashSketch green #2CA02C, FlashBlockRow orange #FF7F0E, GraSS/SJLT black #000000, cuSPARSE red #D62728, FHT purple #5254A3 and Dense Gaussian blue #1F77B4. Marker shape encodes k and line style encodes (κ,s), providing some redundancy, but hue separation is not fully grayscale-safe.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The PDF is predominantly vector: line/bar charts, table rules, labels and captions remain vector objects. Figure 2 is the sole embedded raster image in pdfimages output (1284×642 at roughly 401 dpi); its matrix texture is combined with vector caption/text. All 51 PDF pages, including references and appendices, were rendered at 200 dpi for visual review.
paper_style.style_consistency: PDF text uses Nimbus Roman No9 L/Computer Modern families, while matplotlib plot text is embedded as DejaVu Sans Type 3. Camera-ready plots use source min_font_size=10 with 11-point titles/axes and 9-point legends; ablation plots use the same chart grammar, 2.0-point lines, 0.8-point dispersion outlines and shared external legends. The main/appendix systems are consistent in color, marker and log-axis semantics, with the deliberate exception of the two standalone legends and Figure 4 mixed panels.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Quality–speed Pareto frontier (preview). We compare sketching methods by runtime on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (x-axis) and quality measured using error in Gram matrix approximation (y-axis). Lower is better for both axes. FlashSketch pushes the Pareto frontier.

color.semantic_mapping: FlashSketch (green), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple); marker shape independently encodes k.

encodings.y: Gram Frobenius error (relative), log scale
encodings.color: method family: FlashSketch green versus four baselines (blue, black, red, purple)
encodings.line: method trajectory over k; speedup annotation is an arrow/text comparison
encodings.text: 4.43x speedup annotation and title input shape

figures.data_and_statistics: Representative GPT2-medium stacked-weights primitive sketching result (d=16384, n=1024). The PDF Experimental section states CUDA-event means over 10 post-warm-up iterations in FP32; the source plotting code aggregates mean points and standard-deviation ellipses. No formal interval is shown in the caption.
figures.evidence_relation: The introduction uses this preview to connect the co-design thesis to the Section 7 quality–speed claim. Figures 7–22 expand Gram approximation across inputs and shapes, while Table 1 aggregates all RandNLA tasks.
design_strengths: A single log–log Pareto view makes the lower-is-better trade-off immediately legible.
The two legends separate method identity from k and the arrow makes the headline speedup visible.
Caption states hardware, metric direction, comparison and main finding.
design_weaknesses: The plot is dense for a preview and relies on color plus tiny markers at two-column size.
The caption does not define the marker/line mapping or dispersion ellipses; source and visual cross-reference are needed for full interpretation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a compact log–log error/time Pareto plot with separate method and sketch-dimension legends, one explicit speedup annotation, and a caption that states metric direction.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Example S ∼ BLOCKPERM-SJLT. Sparsity is a union of edge-disjoint permutations (degree-κ regular at the block level). Each block is a sparse JL matrix with s nonzeros per column. Here, M = 16, with block size Br = 64, Bc = 128. The block degree is κ = 4 and the intra-block sparsity is s = 2. The resulting sketch therefore has κs = 8 nonzeros per column, input dimension d = MBc = 2048 and output dimension k = MBr = 1024. Each of the 4 permutations is colored differently for visualization.

color.semantic_mapping: red–white–green sign matrix with translucent tab10 overlays for four edge-disjoint block permutations; block position encodes sparsity wiring

encodings.color: permutation identity and signed nonzero values
encodings.shape: block rectangles encode block support; no point marker semantics
encodings.text: caption provides M, Br, Bc, κ, s, d, k and nonzero count

figures.data_and_statistics: A schematic generated from a 1024×2048 sketch matrix with M=16, Br=64, Bc=128, κ=4 and s=2. The embedded matrix image shows signed nonzeros and translucent permutation overlays; it is not a statistical estimate.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 4 introduces BLOCKPERM-SJLT and Section 5 explains the thread-block kernel. This matrix interface is the visual bridge from the block-permutation construction to the local shared-memory accumulation described by Algorithm 1.
design_strengths: The block support pattern makes locality and edge-disjoint permutation wiring concrete before the kernel details.
Caption is unusually self-contained: it gives construction parameters and the resulting dimensions.
Color overlays preserve a direct mapping from the four permutations to block positions.
design_weaknesses: Rasterized sign texture and translucent colors are not grayscale-safe.
The figure has no legend for permutation colors; readers must use the caption and spatial grouping rather than a keyed color label.
The rectangular matrix is conceptual and does not show the actual tile execution order or memory transactions.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a structured random operator, show block support as a matrix first, then state the block dimensions and degree/sparsity parameters in the caption; use color as a secondary key rather than the only structural cue.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Sketch-and-ridge regression on Qwen2-1.5B stacked weights. We compare end-to-end runtime on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (x-axis) and quality measured using sketch-and-ridge regression residual (y-axis). Lower is better for both axes.

color.semantic_mapping: FlashSketch (green), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple); marker shape independently encodes k.

encodings.y: relative sketch-and-ridge regression residual, log scale
encodings.color: method family: FlashSketch green and four baselines
encodings.line: method trajectory over k; 1.83x speedup arrow/text annotation
encodings.text: 1.83x speedup annotation and Qwen2-1.5B title

figures.data_and_statistics: Representative Qwen2-1.5B stacked-weights sketch-and-ridge result (d=65536, n=512). The source camera-ready plot groups means by method and k and can add standard-deviation ellipses; the PDF caption states the residual and total-time directions but no interval or seed count.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 7.3 points to this object as the representative downstream Pareto frontier; Table 1 aggregates sketch-and-ridge and sketch-and-solve speedups, and Figures 39–54/G.3 expand the residual sweep.
design_strengths: The same two-legend grammar as Figure 1 makes primitive and downstream comparisons visually comparable.
The explicit total-time axis distinguishes application cost from primitive sketch time.
The caption names the input, GPU, residual metric and lower-is-better direction.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits the 1.83x annotation and does not define marker/line semantics.
Residual curves and six k markers are visually crowded at the low-time end.
Shared plotting defaults make the downstream residual look like a primitive Pareto chart even though the solve pipeline changes the cost denominator.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep primitive and downstream quality–time figures structurally aligned, but change the x-axis label to total wall-clock time and state the downstream residual explicitly.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. End-to-end GraSS evaluation on MNIST. We compare sketching methods by sketch runtime per sample on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (x-axis), and quality measured using the LDS metric (y-axis). Lower is better for time (x-axis), higher is better for LDS (y-axis). FlashSketch pushes the Pareto frontier and achieves up to ∼ 3.2× speedup over the GraSS baseline while maintaining attribution quality (top).

color.semantic_mapping: FlashSketch (green), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple); marker shape independently encodes k.

encodings.x: top: Projection time per sample (ms), linear; bottom: categorical k
encodings.y: top: LDS (higher is better); bottom: projection time per sample (ms)
encodings.color: method family: FlashSketch, cuSPARSE, FHT, Dense Gaussian and GraSS
encodings.line: top method trajectories connect k values; bottom bars compare methods at k
encodings.facet: top Pareto scatter and bottom grouped bars
encodings.text: bar labels show ratios/speedups; panel titles state GraSS on MNIST and speedup context

figures.data_and_statistics: Two-panel GraSS-on-MNIST result (d=4k, n=512) on an NVIDIA RTX A6000. The top panel reports projection time per sample versus LDS; the bottom reports projection time bars with error bars and ratio annotations for k=1024, 2048 and 4096. The caption states the LDS direction and up-to-3.2× result.
figures.evidence_relation: Section 7.4 connects the replacement of only the GraSS projection kernel to end-to-end data attribution quality. Appendix E defines the LDS protocol; Table 1 and the RandNLA ablations provide the broader task-level cost context.
design_strengths: The top Pareto panel and bottom cost bars put quality and cost in one object, matching the end-to-end claim.
Error bars and ratio text expose variability and the comparison denominator for the bar panel.
Caption states the hardware, metric directions, baseline comparison and headline speedup.
design_weaknesses: The bottom title says “Speedup relative to GraSS baseline” while its y-axis is projection time per sample; ratio labels and bar height require careful reading.
The top and bottom panels use different x semantics (continuous time versus categorical k), increasing grammar complexity.
Method color is not fully grayscale-safe even though bar position and text provide partial redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a quality–cost scatter with a denominator-explicit bar panel when an end-to-end claim needs both frontier position and baseline-normalized cost; label the two x/y semantics separately.

figures.data_and_statistics: A key-only object with six marker examples and no data values. It is a reproduction aid for every Appendix F/G ablation chart.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 5 is the shared k legend for Figures 7–134; it sits beside the first Appendix F charts but is reused by the RTX A6000 charts in Appendix G.
design_strengths: Separating the six k markers from every plot materially reduces legend duplication.

figures.reusable_pattern: Publish one compact, standalone marker key when the same finite parameter sweep repeats across many small multiples.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6. Legend for methods and parameters. Line colors/styles indicate method families and (κ, s) settings used across the appendix ablations.

color.semantic_mapping: method family color plus line style for κ,s: green FlashSketch, orange FlashBlockRow, black SJLT GraSS Kernel, red SJLT cuSPARSE, purple FHT, blue Dense Gaussian

encodings.color: method family
encodings.line: κ,s parameter variants and SJLT sparsity s
encodings.text: method and parameter labels printed beside line samples

figures.data_and_statistics: A key-only object with method-family swatches and line-style samples; it contains no measurements. It documents the parameter vocabulary used by each ablation chart.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 6 completes the shared legend system with Figure 5 and decodes Figures 7–134; the main plots intentionally suppress local legends to preserve chart area.
design_strengths: Color and line-style redundancy allows variant families to be compared across many plots.
The two-column key groups method family and parameter variants instead of repeating them in every panel.
Source code makes the method colors and line-style lists exact and reproducible.
design_weaknesses: The many variants create a dense key with small labels.
Hue mapping is not grayscale-safe; dashed variants are the only secondary cue.
The caption says colors/styles indicate settings but does not enumerate the exact mapping itself.
figures.reusable_pattern: Move a stable, high-cardinality parameter legend into a dedicated appendix object, then export no-legend small multiples that share it.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. Gram-matrix approximation ablations. Synthetic Gaussian (d=16384, n=1024). GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090.

color.semantic_mapping: FlashSketch (green), FlashBlockRow (orange), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue)

encodings.y: relative Gram Frobenius error, the Gram-matrix approximation metric
encodings.color: FlashSketch (green), FlashBlockRow (orange), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue)
encodings.line: line style encodes κ,s variants: FlashSketch/FlashBlockRow use nine available styles and SJLT variants use s-specific styles
encodings.text: plot title identifies Synthetic Gaussian and shape; caption identifies NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 and task

figures.data_and_statistics: Synthetic Gaussian input with d=16384, n=1024; relative Gram Frobenius error (lower is better) is plotted against wall-clock sketch time (ms). The paper states that CUDA-event timings are means over 10 post-warm-up iterations in FP32. The public plotting source groups available rows by method/configuration and k, draws mean points and connects k values; translucent ellipses encode one standard deviation in the plotted coordinates, not a confidence interval. The caption gives no seed count or failure-value convention.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix F.2 extends the Section 7 sketch-quality comparison to Synthetic Gaussian at this shape on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090. The external Figures 5–6 legends decode k, method family, and (κ,s); Figures 1/Table 1 provide the main Pareto and aggregate context.
design_strengths: The title and caption bind the task, input (Synthetic Gaussian, d=16384, n=1024), hardware (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090), and metric to the plotted object.
Log scales expose the multiplicative time/error trade-off across orders of magnitude, and marker shape plus line style separate k and (κ,s).
Mean points, connecting trajectories, and translucent dispersion ellipses preserve both Pareto direction and run variability without adding panels.
design_weaknesses: The chart has no local legend: interpreting color, line style, and marker requires Figures 5–6, which increases cross-page lookup cost.
The caption does not define the translucent standard-deviation ellipses or report the run/seed denominator; the visual evidence is therefore less self-contained than the main figures.
Two-column scaling leaves dense variants and small tick labels competing for attention, especially for the high-dimensional or SuiteSparse cases.
figures.reusable_pattern: Reuse one log–log error-versus-sketch-time grammar while changing only input shape and GPU; keep the external k/method legends stable across the ablation grid.

encodings.color: FlashSketch (green), FlashBlockRow (orange), SJLT GraSS Kernel (black), SJLT cuSPARSE (red), Subsampled Fast Hadamard Transform (purple), Dense Gaussian/cuBLAS (blue)
encodings.line: line style encodes κ,s variants: FlashSketch/FlashBlockRow use nine available styles and SJLT variants use s-specific styles
encodings.text: plot title identifies SuiteSparse - spal 004 and shape; caption identifies NVIDIA RTX A6000 and task

figures.data_and_statistics: SuiteSparse - spal 004 input with d=262144, n=512; relative residual (lower is better) is plotted against wall-clock total time (ms). The paper states that CUDA-event timings are means over 10 post-warm-up iterations in FP32. The public plotting source groups available rows by method/configuration and k, draws mean points and connects k values; translucent ellipses encode one standard deviation in the plotted coordinates, not a confidence interval. The caption gives no seed count or failure-value convention.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix G.4 carries the sketch-and-solve residual comparison to SuiteSparse - spal 004 at this shape on NVIDIA RTX A6000. Figures 5–6 decode the parameter sweep and Table 1 gives the aggregate task-level speedups.
design_strengths: The title and caption bind the task, input (SuiteSparse - spal 004, d=262144, n=512), hardware (NVIDIA RTX A6000), and metric to the plotted object.
Log scales expose the multiplicative time/error trade-off across orders of magnitude, and marker shape plus line style separate k and (κ,s).
Mean points, connecting trajectories, and translucent dispersion ellipses preserve both Pareto direction and run variability without adding panels.
design_weaknesses: The chart has no local legend: interpreting color, line style, and marker requires Figures 5–6, which increases cross-page lookup cost.
The caption does not define the translucent standard-deviation ellipses or report the run/seed denominator; the visual evidence is therefore less self-contained than the main figures.
Two-column scaling leaves dense variants and small tick labels competing for attention, especially for the high-dimensional or SuiteSparse cases.
figures.reusable_pattern: Reuse the downstream residual/time grammar from ridge regression while keeping metric labels and external parameter legends consistent across shapes and hardware.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Geomean speedups of FLASHSKETCH vs baselines aggregated over shapes, datasets and configs. Global geomean vs next best baseline: 1.73x.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty intervals, standard deviations, ranks or failure cells are shown; entries are geometric-mean speedups.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four task rows (Gram matrix approximation, OSE, sketch-and-ridge regression, Sketch+Solve) compare FlashSketch against four baseline columns: SJLT (cuSPARSE), SJLT (GraSS Kernel), Subsampled FHT and Dense Gaussian (cuBLAS). Values use two decimal places and aggregate over shapes, datasets and configurations; the caption reports the global geomean versus the next-best baseline as 1.73x.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 1 is the aggregate decision surface for the Section 7 RandNLA comparison. Figures 1 and 3 show representative quality–time frontiers, Figures 7–70/G.1–G.4 unpack task/shape variation, and Figure 4 supplies the separate GraSS end-to-end result.
design_strengths: A compact five-column table puts task-level cost comparison and the global headline in one view.
Two-decimal precision is consistent across all 16 baseline cells.
Booktabs rules and cmidrules separate four task rows without a heavy grid.
design_weaknesses: The table contains speedup aggregates but no denominator counts, variability or failure indicators.
The header is single-level and long method names wrap, so baseline implementation details compete with task labels.
The global 1.73x caption claim is not reproduced in a highlighted cell, requiring a caption read.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a minimal booktabs aggregate table for a headline geomean, while leaving shape-level quality/time evidence to shared-grammar plots.

evidence.label: Table 1 body, header, caption and rules

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The visual narrative moves from the Figure 1 quality–speed claim, through the Figure 2 block-permutation interface, to the Figure 3 downstream residual frontier, Table 1 aggregate speedups and Figure 4 GraSS end-to-end quality/cost. Appendix F/G then expand each RandNLA task over 16 input shapes on RTX 4090/A6000, with Figures 5–6 acting as shared decoding keys.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use a stable “Figure N. bold task/title. dataset (d,n). GPU” construction for the ablation grid and longer setup/comparison/finding prose for main objects. Main captions state metric directions and headline findings where applicable; ablation captions omit the shared legend and dispersion definitions, so they are visually complete only with Figures 5–6.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Table 1 uses one header row: Task, SJLT (cuSPARSE), SJLT (GraSS Kernel), Subsampled FHT and Dense Gaussian (cuBLAS). Four task rows are separated by cmidrules; all cells use two decimals and no uncertainty/failure column.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 2 defines the structured sketch/kernel interface; Figure 1 and Figure 3 show representative quality–time outcomes; Table 1 and Figure 4 connect those outcomes to aggregate RandNLA and GraSS costs; F/G ablations vary task, data shape, k and (κ,s) while preserving the same visual encoding.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main objects are explicit entry points into Appendix F/G: Figure 1 points to Gram ablations, Figure 3 points to downstream residual ablations, Table 1 aggregates all four RandNLA tasks, and Figure 4 is protocol-expanded by Appendix E. Figures 5–6 provide the cross-page legend needed to read F/G.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern in paper text and DejaVu Sans in matplotlib objects are stable across main and appendix; font size compresses in the two-column PDF but source generators keep common 10–11 point chart labels and 8–9 point table/legend text.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Method-family colors and k marker order are reused across Figures 1, 3, 4 and Figures 6–134. Line style is a second encoding for κ,s in ablations. The palette is semantically stable but not completely grayscale-safe, with Figure 2 using a separate red-white-green sign/overlay scheme.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a two-axis log Pareto chart for multiplicative quality/time comparisons, with method color, k marker shape and one explicit speedup annotation.
Export stable high-cardinality legends as standalone appendix figures, then use no-legend small multiples for shape/task/hardware sweeps.
Bind every ablation caption to task, dataset, d, n and GPU while holding chart grammar constant across metrics.
Pair an end-to-end frontier with a baseline-normalized cost bar panel when quality and operational cost are both part of the claim.
failure_patterns: The 128 ablation charts depend on remote Figures 5–6 for legend semantics; captions do not define the ellipses or variant mapping.
A high-cardinality color/line-style system is not fully grayscale-safe and becomes small after two-column scaling.
Table 1 omits variability, denominator counts and failure indicators, while Figure 4 mixes projection-time bars with speedup wording.
The long appendix repeats nearly identical single-panel objects, increasing navigation cost and making cross-panel synthesis dependent on the reader.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: FlashSketch uses a stable, source-reproducible method/color/marker grammar to make quality–time Pareto claims concrete in the main paper, then expands the same grammar across task, input-shape and GPU ablations with shared legends and a compact aggregate table.
